metadata.name: Infectious gastroenteritis
metadata.emergency_level: Usually routine/self-limiting - but dehydration and dysentery/sepsis can be serious
metadata.severity: Usually mild and self-limiting; risk from dehydration, especially extremes of age

overview.short_description: Acute infection of the gastrointestinal tract causing diarrhoea and/or vomiting, usually viral and self-limiting, whose main risk is dehydration.
overview.detailed_description: Gastroenteritis is very common and usually caused by viruses (norovirus, rotavirus) or bacteria (Campylobacter, Salmonella, E. coli) or, less often, parasites. Most cases are self-limiting and managed with fluids (oral rehydration). The main tasks are preventing/treating dehydration, recognising features suggesting invasive/bacterial disease or a non-infective cause, using antibiotics selectively, and infection control (including notification of certain organisms).
overview.pathophysiology: Enteropathogens cause fluid loss via secretory or osmotic mechanisms (viruses/toxins) or mucosal invasion/inflammation (invasive bacteria - dysentery), producing diarrhoea +/- vomiting and, if severe, dehydration and electrolyte disturbance.
overview.etiology: Viral (norovirus, rotavirus, adenovirus), bacterial (Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, E. coli including toxin-producing, C. difficile with antibiotics), and parasitic (Giardia, Cryptosporidium); often food/water-borne or person-to-person.
overview.incubation_period: Hours to a few days depending on pathogen (toxin-mediated food poisoning can be very rapid).
overview.natural_history: Most resolve within a few days to a week; some bacterial/parasitic infections last longer.
overview.prognosis: Excellent in healthy adults; serious in infants, the elderly, and immunocompromised (dehydration/complications).

prevalence.value: Extremely common; a leading cause of illness and, globally, of childhood death from dehydration.

incidence.value: Very high; outbreaks common (norovirus in closed settings).

mortality.value: Low in healthy adults; significant global paediatric mortality from dehydration.

epidemiology.age_groups: All ages; most dangerous at extremes of age.
epidemiology.geographic_distribution: Worldwide; higher burden with poor sanitation.
epidemiology.seasonal_pattern: Norovirus in winter; some bacterial causes in warmer months.

risk_factors.lifestyle: Contaminated food/water, poor hand hygiene, close-contact settings.
risk_factors.diabetes: May worsen with illness (dehydration, glycaemic control).
risk_factors.occupation: Food handlers, healthcare/childcare workers (transmission and exclusion rules).
risk_factors.medications: Recent antibiotics (C. difficile), acid suppression (increased susceptibility), immunosuppressants.

symptoms.importance: Suggests invasive bacterial infection - RED FLAG (also consider IBD)

symptoms.symptom: Signs of dehydration (thirst, reduced urine, dizziness, lethargy)

negative_findings.finding: No dehydration, no blood in stool, systemically well
negative_findings.why_important: Supports simple self-limiting viral gastroenteritis managed at home

negative_findings.finding: No severe/localised abdominal pain or peritonism
negative_findings.why_important: Argues against a surgical abdomen (e.g., appendicitis) presenting with GI symptoms

history_questions.question: How much diarrhoea/vomiting, and are you able to keep fluids down and passing urine?
Any blood in the stool, high fever, or severe/localised abdominal pain?
history_questions.why_ask: Screens for invasive infection or surgical cause

history_questions.question: Recent travel, suspect food, contacts, or antibiotics?
Are you a food handler/healthcare/childcare worker, and any vulnerable contacts?
Any comorbidity/immunosuppression, pregnancy, or extremes of age?

physical_examination.examination: Hydration assessment (pulse, BP/postural drop, mucous membranes, capillary refill, skin turgor)

physical_examination.expected_finding: Generalised mild tenderness; localised/peritonitic signs suggest another cause

physical_examination.examination: Temperature and general appearance / sepsis screen

laboratory_tests.indication: Blood in stool, severe/persistent illness, immunocompromise, recent travel/antibiotics, public-health need

imaging.when_needed: Only if surgical/other abdominal pathology suspected

other_diagnostic_tests.culture: Stool culture as above; C. difficile testing if recent antibiotics/hospital

diagnostic_criteria.formal_criteria: Clinical diagnosis: acute onset diarrhoea +/- vomiting, usually with a compatible history (food/contacts/travel) and no features of an alternative/surgical cause. Stool testing is selective (not routine for simple cases). Assess dehydration and severity.

differential_diagnosis.differences: Chronic/recurrent, blood, systemic features, drug history
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Is this a new acute illness or a chronic/recurrent problem?

differential_diagnosis.differences: Localised/severe pain, peritonism, no significant diarrhoea
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Is the pain severe and localised rather than crampy with diarrhoea?
Are you systemically very unwell with signs of sepsis?

differential_diagnosis.disease: Other causes of vomiting (DKA, raised ICP, etc.)
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Any diabetes, headache, or other features rather than a GI bug?

diagnostic_questions.question: Are you able to keep fluids down and are you passing urine (hydration)?
diagnostic_questions.interpretation: Unable to maintain hydration / signs of dehydration -> escalate care

diagnostic_questions.question: Is there blood in the stool or high fever (invasive/dysenteric features)?
diagnostic_questions.interpretation: Bloody diarrhoea/high fever -> stool testing, assess for antibiotics/complications

next_best_question.question: Can you keep fluids down, any blood in stool/high fever, and any high-risk features (age, immunosuppression, travel)?
next_best_question.expected_answers: Simple case vs red flags/high risk
next_best_question.branching_logic: Well, hydrated, no red flags -> oral rehydration + safety-net; dehydration/dysentery/high-risk -> assess, stool tests, consider fluids/antibiotics/admission

next_best_test.why: Blood in stool, severe/persistent, travel, immunocompromise, or public health

red_flags.finding: Signs of significant dehydration or shock (especially infants/elderly)
red_flags.immediate_action: Urgent rehydration (IV if needed) and assessment/admission

red_flags.finding: Bloody diarrhoea with high fever / systemic illness (dysentery/sepsis)
red_flags.immediate_action: Assess urgently; stool testing; consider antibiotics/admission

red_flags.finding: Severe or localised abdominal pain / peritonism
Prolonged illness (>1-2 weeks) or immunocompromised patient

referral_criteria.urgent_referral: Significant dehydration/shock; suspected surgical abdomen or sepsis; vulnerable patient unable to maintain hydration.
referral_criteria.routine_referral: Persistent diarrhoea for investigation; suspected non-infective cause.

late: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome (E. coli O157 - do NOT give antibiotics if suspected)

initial_management.supportive_care: Maintain hydration - oral rehydration solution, small frequent sips; continue eating as tolerated; rest; strict hand hygiene and infection control (stay off work/school until 48 hours after symptoms settle).
initial_management.medications: Canonical schema 1.3 guidance: use treatment_guidance.medication_options and its history-based safety checks. Candidate classes/options (not a prescription): Oral rehydration solution; Loperamide; Pathogen-directed antimicrobial. No autonomous selection or dosing is allowed. Source IDs: IDSA_DIARRHEA_2017.
initial_management.lifestyle_advice: Hydration, hygiene, food safety; exclusion for food handlers/healthcare workers per local rules; notify notifiable organisms.
initial_management.follow_up: Safety-net for dehydration/deterioration; investigate persistent symptoms.
initial_management.legacy_medications_pre_v13: Usually none; oral rehydration is key. Antiemetics/antidiarrhoeals used cautiously (avoid loperamide in dysentery/possible invasive infection or children). ANTIBIOTICS ONLY when indicated (severe/invasive bacterial infection, specific pathogens, high-risk patients) - avoid empirical antibiotics in simple cases and if E. coli O157 possible.

patient_education.home_advice: A tummy bug usually clears on its own in a few days. The most important thing is to keep drinking - take small frequent sips of water or oral rehydration solution and keep eating if you can. Wash your hands well and stay off work/school until 48 hours after the diarrhoea and vomiting stop. Get medical help if you can't keep fluids down, pass little urine, feel very unwell, or have blood in your stool.
patient_education.home_advice_ar: النزلة المعوية تزول عادةً وحدها خلال أيام. الأهم هو الاستمرار في الشرب - رشفات صغيرة متكرّرة من الماء أو محلول الإماهة الفموي مع الأكل قدر الإمكان. اغسل يديك جيداً والزم المنزل حتى 48 ساعة بعد توقّف الإسهال والقيء. اطلب المساعدة الطبية إذا لم تستطع الاحتفاظ بالسوائل، أو قلّ التبوّل، أو شعرت بتوعّك شديد، أو ظهر دم في البراز.
patient_education.prevention: Hand hygiene, safe food/water, and (for children) rotavirus vaccination.
patient_education.warning_signs: Unable to keep fluids down, reduced urine, dizziness, blood in stool, high fever, severe abdominal pain, or a very unwell child/elderly person.

prevention.vaccination: Rotavirus vaccine (infants); typhoid/cholera vaccines for travel where relevant.
prevention.lifestyle: Hand hygiene, safe food and water, food-handler hygiene.
prevention.screening: Not applicable (public-health surveillance/notification for certain organisms).

evidence.evidence_level: High for oral rehydration; selective antibiotic use.
evidence.guideline_strength: The main diagnosis/test and treatment direction was checked against the current guidance identified by IDSA_DIARRHEA_2017; see evidence_review for scope and limitations. This does not verify every legacy narrative sentence.

limitations: Guidelines require individual clinical judgement and may differ by country, formulary and antimicrobial resistance.
The evidence audit verifies traceability and major safety structure; it does not certify every narrative sentence.
No medication should be selected or dosed without patient-specific contraindication and interaction checking.

treatment_guidance.treatment_goal: Prevent/treat dehydration, identify invasive disease and restrict antimicrobials to defined indications.
treatment_guidance.legacy_narrative_summary: Canonical schema 1.3 guidance: use treatment_guidance.medication_options and its history-based safety checks. Candidate classes/options (not a prescription): Oral rehydration solution; Loperamide; Pathogen-directed antimicrobial. No autonomous selection or dosing is allowed. Source IDs: IDSA_DIARRHEA_2017.
required_history_before_any_medication: age and weight where dosing is weight- or age-dependent
pregnancy or breastfeeding status when relevant
documented drug allergies and the exact reaction
all prescribed, OTC, herbal and recreational substances
major cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal and bleeding history
non_drug_measures: Continue appropriate nutrition, hand hygiene and public-health advice; use sick-day medicine review when dehydrated.

medication_options.when_to_consider: Mild-moderate dehydration when oral route is safe
medication_options.dose_policy: Dose is not inferred from this KB; use age, weight, renal/hepatic function, pregnancy status and the current local formulary/medicine label.

avoid_if: unsafe oral route because of shock, ileus, altered consciousness or persistent uncontrollable vomiting
use_caution_if: heart failure, advanced renal disease, severe electrolyte disturbance, diabetes, or need for precisely controlled fluids
monitoring: hydration, urine output, weight and electrolytes when clinically indicated

medication_options.when_to_consider: Watery diarrhoea only after excluding invasive/C. difficile disease
medication_options.dose_policy: Dose is not inferred from this KB; use age, weight, renal/hepatic function, pregnancy status and the current local formulary/medicine label.

avoid_if: bloody diarrhoea, high fever, suspected invasive infection/C. difficile, ileus, toxic megacolon, or young child without specialist direction
use_caution_if: liver disease, acute ulcerative colitis flare, dehydration, or uncertain diagnosis
monitoring: stop if worsening pain/distension, fever, blood or lack of improvement

medication_options.when_to_consider: Severe/invasive disease, defined pathogen, traveller/high-risk indication or specialist/public-health advice
medication_options.dose_policy: Dose is not inferred from this KB; use age, weight, renal/hepatic function, pregnancy status and the current local formulary/medicine label.

avoid_if: documented immediate or severe delayed penicillin allergy
use_caution_if: renal impairment, prior C. difficile, or recent antibiotic exposure
monitoring: clinical response, allergy and antibiotic-associated diarrhoea

avoid_if: prior serious macrolide allergy or clinically important QT prolongation with interacting drugs
use_caution_if: liver disease, bradycardia, hypokalaemia, myasthenia gravis, pregnancy, or QT-prolonging medicines
monitoring: clinical response; ECG/electrolytes when risk is material

medication_options.clinical_note: Avoid empiric therapy when STEC is possible; use local microbiology/resistance advice.

procedures_referral_and_escalation: Hospital care for shock, severe dehydration, altered consciousness, peritonism, severe bloody diarrhoea, sepsis or high-risk host.
treatment_guidance.localization_note: Before use in Libya, align choices with the Libyan formulary, local availability, antimicrobial resistance, referral pathways and prescribing law.
